task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-06-16, in the area of defensive suppression and counter strategy (best/avoid)):
Adhering to a suppression-conditional recommended mix predicts winning.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): 54 series

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

methodological_questions: Is the recommended mix derived independently of the outcome it is meant to predict (leakage, outcome-derived labels)?
Does adherence predict winning after controlling for team quality and opponent?
Does adherence beat a placebo or baseline such as the team's modal play type or a random mix?
How are score-state reverse causation and multiple testing handled?

historical_evidence.finding: The engine's top recommended play type was compared with the team's modal play type in playoff series. The calibrated headline hit rate was 69.8% (37/53). Comparisons against a banned-PT DRIVE-modal were 85.7% (12/14) and clean comparisons were 64.1% (25/39). The uncalibrated archival rate was 51.7% (31/60). Recorded failure mechanism: C_artifact. Limits: small sample. Risks: leakage/lookahead and sample size. No bootstrap CI was computed.

Ranked playsheet validation on 10 series. The full-rank Spearman was null (rho=-0.0639, p=0.0997, n=665). The pairwise comparison BEST 1.257 PPP (n=56) vs AVOID 1.092 PPP (n=160) gave Mann-Whitney p=0.004. Limits recorded: leakage, low measurement reliability, small sample. Risks recorded include drift/nonstationarity.

The Possession Control Index gain over ORtg was driven by a leakage component that tracks DRtg (corr +0.894). The offensive-control increment was dR2=+0.005. The baseline omitted defense by construction (Net=ORtg-DRtg). Risks recorded: leakage/lookahead and mechanical floor.

A proxy matchup-conditioned play-type picker showed a possession-level gain (C gamma +0.0714 PPP, n=16,921 cells), but proxy agreement with the production engine was only 16.5% (13/79). Recorded problems: in-sample contamination of regular-season aggregates, iid standard errors, and coverage of only 35.7% clear recommendations.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Series-level hit rate of the engine's recommendation versus the team's modal play type
failed_approaches.why: Recorded as an artifact from a construction, selection or labelling flaw. Limits were small sample (n=53) and leakage/lookahead, with no CI.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Ranked BEST>SECOND>AVOID playsheet validation on 10 series
failed_approaches.why: The full-rank signal was null. [prior work] cites leakage, low measurement reliability and small sample as limits, and the mechanism is recorded as unclear.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Outcome-linked composite index evaluated against Net Rating
failed_approaches.why: Leakage tracked DRtg and the baseline omitted defense by construction. This is the recorded mechanical-floor/leakage artifact.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Proxy engine evaluated on all regular-season games
failed_approaches.why: Proxy fidelity was 16.5%, regular-season aggregates were contaminated in-sample, and the standard errors were iid.

evidence_establishes: Earlier work on closely related recommendation-quality questions found no clean positive result. Two of the four retrieved records are recorded as artifact and two as inconclusive.
Apparent positive signals (69.8% hit rate, pairwise BEST>AVOID, +0.07 PPP) coincided with recorded leakage, small-sample, or proxy-fidelity limits.
Series-level validation with about 53 scoreable units has been tried and was recorded as limited by small sample and leakage.
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether adherence to a recommended mix, measured as actual play-type shares, predicts winning. The retrieved records test recommendation hit rates or PPP, not adherence-to-win.
Whether a leakage-free, pre-registered version of the recommendation has any predictive value.
Any effect size for adherence on win probability net of team strength.
own_inferences: The question as posed is ambiguous. 'Adherence' and 'predicts winning' are undefined, and the recommendation is likely derived from the same series it would be tested on, which is outcome-derived by construction.

Adherence probably correlates with winning through team quality, score state (leading teams run different play types) and the opponent's suppression itself, so an unconditioned association would likely be an artifact.
54 series cannot detect modest effects. A game-level analysis with series clustering gives more observations but only modest effective power.
The base expectation, given [prior work], is that a naive test shows a positive association that shrinks or vanishes after leakage and team-strength controls.
uncertainties: The 54 series are not decomposed by season. It is unclear whether they include partial 2025-26 playoffs, which complete only on 2026-06-21, after the question date.
The exact definition of the 'suppression-conditional recommended mix' and how it is generated are not given in the task.
Records are truncated ('cut'), so details of the retrieved studies were not read in full.
Whether the engine's recommendations can be reconstructed using only pre-series information is unknown.

historical_effect.explanation: Without history one might proceed with a straightforward adherence-vs-win regression. [prior work] show repeated leakage and artifact outcomes in this area, so the decision moves to proceed_with_changes with strict ex-ante recommendation freezing, team-strength controls, placebo mixes and a locked confirmatory holdout, and lower expected support.
